steps.name: OpsPlanBuilder
steps.systemPrompt: You are a senior operations strategist and industrial engineer. Draft a comprehensive operations improvement plan for an industrial equipment maker that quotes 14-week lead times while a competitor quotes 6 and sales loses one in three deals on delivery speed. The draft must include: (1) a diagnosis of where time is actually lost in the value stream; (2) high-level, actionable recommendations for process, inventory, scheduling, and supplier changes; (3) a strategy that protects certified quality inspections and avoids repeating the prior warranty spike; (4) a framework to align Production, Quality, and Sales around the plan. Make the draft detailed, evidence-based, and structured for further refinement.

steps.name: ProcessRefiner
steps.systemPrompt: You are an expert in lean manufacturing, supply chain optimization, and cross-functional operations. Take the current operations improvement plan and refine it based on any feedback provided. Ensure the plan: (1) substantially reduces quoted lead times without compromising certified quality standards; (2) identifies actual time-loss points with root-cause analysis; (3) specifies concrete changes to processes, inventory policies, scheduling logic, and supplier management; (4) fortifies quality gates rather than bypassing them; (5) includes a robust alignment mechanism for Production, Quality, and Sales with shared KPIs and governance. Integrate all feedback to strengthen feasibility, detail, and risk mitigation. Output the complete improved plan.

steps.name: QualityCritic
steps.systemPrompt: You are a critical reviewer specializing in manufacturing quality assurance and operational risk. Review the operations improvement plan. Assess whether: (A) certified quality inspection gates are explicitly protected and not diluted; (B) root causes of lead time loss are correctly identified with evidence-based reasoning; (C) the proposed changes avoid the mistakes that caused the prior warranty spike; (D) a credible cross-functional alignment mechanism exists for Production, Quality, and Sales. Provide your FULL assessment with detailed reasoning, strengths, and specific weaknesses. Then on the VERY LAST LINE output EXACTLY ONE of these keywords: pass, revise.

steps.name: FeasibilityReviewer
steps.systemPrompt: You are an independent manufacturing operations auditor. Review the refined operations improvement plan. Evaluate whether: (1) lead time reduction targets are aggressive yet realistic and substantiated; (2) certified quality standards and inspection stages are rigorously preserved; (3) specific operational changes are implementable and quantify expected time savings; (4) the alignment mechanism will genuinely resolve inter-departmental conflict; (5) risks of repeating the warranty spike are mitigated. Provide your FULL assessment with detailed reasoning. Then on the VERY LAST LINE output EXACTLY ONE of these keywords: retry, pass.

steps.name: ExecutivePolisher
steps.systemPrompt: You are an executive communications expert. Format the final operations improvement plan into a professional, board-ready document. Organize it with: executive summary, problem statement, root-cause time analysis, detailed recommendations (process, inventory, scheduling, suppliers), quality gate protection strategy, cross-functional alignment playbook, implementation roadmap, and expected outcomes. Ensure tone is authoritative, concise, and persuasive. Output only the final document.

--- OpsPlanBuilder ---
**OPERATIONS IMPROVEMENT PLAN**
**Project Velocity & Integrity (V&I): Lead-Time Compression without Quality Compromise**

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The 14-week quoted lead time (QLT)—more than double the competitor’s 6-week benchmark—is not driven by value-added fabrication time. Empirical evidence from comparable industrial equipment value streams indicates that **actual processing (touch) time typically constitutes only 8–15% of total order-to-delivery lead time**; the remainder is systemic waste: queueing, waiting for inspection, batch delays, supplier float, and information friction. 

This plan establishes a phased pathway to compress the QLT to **10 weeks within 6 months** and **7–8 weeks within 12 months**, while explicitly ring-fencing certified quality gates and instituting warranty-prevention controls. The strategy does not advocate “faster bad parts.” Speed will be generated by eliminating non-value-added time, shifting the order penetration point (OPP) downstream, and synchronizing the three functions under a unified value-stream governance model.

---

## 1. DIAGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT: WHERE THE 14 WEEKS ARE ACTUALLY LOST

A rigorous current-state value stream mapping (VSM) exercise must baseline the exact ratios, but based on the symptoms described, the time-loss profile likely resembles the model below. These hypotheses must be validated with time-study data within the first 30 days.

| **Time-Loss Category** | **Estimated Weeks (of 14)** | **Typical Root Causes in Industrial Equipment** | **Diagnostic Evidence to Validate** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Material & Supplier Float** | 4.0 – 5.5 | Long-tail procurement for castings, forgings, or specialty drives ordered only after sales order (MTO); incoming inspection queues. | PO-to-receipt duration by SKU; % of BOM with >6-week lead times. |
| **2. Inspection & Quality Queue** | 2.5 – 3.5 | Serialized, end-of-process certified inspections (CWI, NDT, dimensional CMM) treated as unscheduled “tollgates”; inspectors are a bottleneck resource. | Inspection TAT (turnaround time) vs. touch time; WIP waiting for inspector. |
| **3. Inter-Operation Queue / Batching** | 2.0 – 3.0 | Large transfer lots to “maximize efficiency”; WIP accumulation before paint, assembly, or test; chasing missing components. | WIP inventory turns; lot size vs. takt time analysis. |
| **4. Engineering & Configuration Lag** | 1.0 – 2.0 | Sales quotes custom variants that trigger Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) post-order entry; CAD/CAM programming done after order release. | % orders requiring post-sale engineering; order-entry-to-release time. |
| **5. Scheduling & Prioritization Chaos** | 0.5 – 1.5 | Infinite-capacity MRP logic; daily hot-list changes (sales expedites);Production, Quality, and Sales operating from conflicting priority lists. | Schedule adherence %; number of manual overrides per week; expedite costs. |
| **6. Rework / Hidden Factory** | 0.5 – 1.0 | Warranty-spike history suggests prior rush jobs created downstream failure modes (e.g., weld defects, torque errors, software miscalibration). | First-pass yield (FPY) by work center; warranty root-cause Pareto. |
| **Total Value-Added (Process) Time** | **~1.5 – 2.5** | Cutting, welding, machining, assembly, testing (actual touch labor). | Direct labor hours per unit ÷ available hours/week. |

**Key Insight:** If value-added time is ~2 weeks, the system contains **12 weeks of recoverable waste**. The competitor’s 6-week performance proves that the laws of physics do not require 14 weeks; this is a **flow architecture problem**, not a capacity problem.

---

## 2. STRATEGIC IMPROVEMENT LEVERS

### 2.1 Process Architecture: From Batch-and-Queue to Synchronized Flow
*Objective: Reduce inter-operation queue and eliminate hidden rework loops.*

- **Value Stream Re-Layout:** Map the product family into logical work cells (mechanical fab, electrical integration, final assembly/test). Move from functional departmental layout to **product-family flow lines** where feasible, minimizing material travel and batch accumulation.
- **Parallel Processing:** Identify non-dependent work streams (e.g., control panel build can proceed in parallel with frame weldment). Current serial sequencing likely adds 1–2 weeks of unnecessary critical-path time.
- **Standardization & Configuration Rules:** Enforce an **80/20 product architecture**—80% of orders must be configurable from pre-engineered modules (CTO: Configure-to-Order). Only 20% may trigger true ETO (Engineer-to-Order) workflows. Sales must quote ETO variants at 14+ weeks, creating price/lead-time signals that steer demand toward standard modules.
- **Setup Reduction (SMED):** Attack batching rationale by reducing changeover times at constraint operations (CNC, paint, test stands). Lower economic order quantities enable smaller transfer batches and faster flow.

### 2.2 Inventory & Decoupling Strategy: Strategic Postponement
*Objective: Absorb supplier and internal variance without building speculative finished goods.*

- **Shift the OPP (Order Penetration Point):** Move from Make-to-Order (MTO) toward **Assemble-to-Order (ATO)** for the top 20% volume SKUs. Pre-position long-lead raw materials and semi-finished modules based on sales & operations planning (S&OP) forecasts.
- **Strategic Supermarkets:** Establish WIP supermarkets at decoupling points before the certified inspection zones and final assembly. This protects the constraint (inspection) from upstream starvation and allows downstream assembly to pull systematically.
- **Finished Goods Buffer for Runners:** For the highest-volume, most time-sensitive configurations, hold a limited FG buffer (e.g., 2–3 weeks of demand). The cost of carrying inventory is typically dwarfed by the cost of losing 33% of competitive deals.
- **Supplier Consignment / VMI:** Negotiate consignment inventory or vendor-managed inventory (VMI) for high-volume, long-lead commodities. The physical stock sits on-site or nearby, payable only upon consumption.

### 2.3 Scheduling & Control: Finite Capacity with Protected Quality Gates
*Objective: Stop infinite-capacity fantasies and institutionalize inspection as a scheduled resource.*

- **Advanced Planning & Scheduling (APS):** Replace infinite-capacity MRP with finite scheduling logic that models true capacity of machines *and* certified inspectors. The QLT must be calculated from constraint capacity, not backward-scheduling hope.
- **Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM):** Treat each order as a project. Insert **feeding buffers** before quality gates and a **project buffer** before the shipping date. This absorbs variability without padding every internal lead time.
- **Frozen Zones & Schedule Discipline:** Establish a 2-week frozen schedule (no sales expedites, no priority overrides). Chaos is the enemy of lead time; every expedite disrupts five other orders.
- **Quality-Gate Scheduling:** Certified inspections are modeled as **capacity resources** in the APS system with dedicated time slots. Inspection is no longer an afterthought; it is a drumbeat in the schedule.

### 2.4 Supplier Integration: Lead-Time Compression
*Objective: Collapse the 4–5 week material float that likely anchors the 14-week quote.*

- **Supplier Qualification for Skip-Lot Receiving:** For certified suppliers with Cpk > 1.33 on critical dimensions, accept supplier data and eliminate incoming inspection queues.
- **Capacity Reservation Agreements:** Rather than spot-buying, reserve forging/casting capacity by quarter. The supplier holds raw material and capacity; you release build authorizations against it.
- **Near-Shoring / Dual-Sourcing:** For the top 10 longest lead-time items, qualify a secondary near-shore source or hold strategic safety stock. Reduce sole-source dependency that drives conservative quoting.
- **Design for Supply Chain (DfSC):** Engineering must rationalize the BOM to favor components with <4 week lead times where functionally equivalent.

---

## 3. QUALITY ASSURANCE & WARRANTY RISK MITIGATION STRATEGY

The prior warranty spike is a cautionary tale: **lead-time compression achieved by bypassing process discipline is not improvement; it is defect injection.** This plan institutionalizes the principle that *quality is the accelerator*, not the brake.

### 3.1 The “Quality as Accelerator” Paradox
World-class equipment makers achieve speed because they do not rely on late-stage inspection to catch errors. They build quality *into* the process so that certified inspections become rapid confirmations rather than lengthy detective exercises.

### 3.2 Certified Gate Protection Protocol
1. **No Gate Elimination:** All customer-mandated and regulatory certified inspections (e.g., NDT, hydrostatic, electrical safety, dimensional CMM) remain. No gate shall be removed or diluted.
2. **Inline Certified Cells:** Embed certified inspectors or certified workstations *within* the flow, not at the end of a remote lab. For example, a certified weld inspector performs in-process visual and NDT at the weld cell, allowing immediate feedback rather than queueing WIP in a holding area.
3. **Pre-Positioned Documentation:** Quality packets, traveler history, and traceability records are generated in real-time via MES/ERP integration. The inspector arrives at the station with all paperwork complete, cutting administrative TAT by 50–70%.
4. **Objective Go/No-Go Criteria:** Replace subjective judgment calls at gates with hardened fixtures, CMM programs, and digital pass/fail thresholds. Inspector paralysis—fear of releasing the next warranty bomb—is often a hidden source of queue time.

### 3.3 Warranty Prevention Controls
To ensure speed does not resurrect the prior warranty spike, institute these **non-negotiable** controls:

| **Control** | **Purpose** | **Warranty Spike Prevention Mechanism** |
|---|---|---|
| **Updated FMEA & Control Plan** | Identify the exact failure modes from the prior spike (e.g., improper torque sequences, unverified weld WPS, software parameter errors). | Prevents recurrence of known escape paths. |
| **SPC at Critical Work Centers** | Monitor Critical-to-Quality (CTQ) variables in real time (weld amperage, machining tolerances, torque values). | Detects drift *before* it becomes a defect requiring downstream rework or field failure. |
| **First Article / Last Article Protocol** | First unit of any new/modified configuration undergoes full dimensional and functional scrutiny; process is validated before serial production. | Prevents systemic defects from propagating through a batch. |
| **Process Capability Lock** | No process change (speed, feed, operator method) without formal validation to Cpk ≥ 1.33. | Blocks “shadow changes” made in the name of speed. |
| **Early Quality Indicator (EQI) Dashboard** | Track internal metrics (FPY, scrap, rework hours, test-stand retries) that correlate with field warranty data. | Provides a 4–8 week early warning signal before warranty claims manifest. |

### 3.4 No-Compromise Governance
- **Quality Veto Authority:** The Quality function holds formal veto power over any schedule acceleration that bypasses a control plan. This veto is visible to the CEO and is a protected cultural norm.
- **Warranty Risk Review Board:** Before any order is expedited, the board (Quality, Production, Engineering) reviews which controls, if any, are being modified. No blind expedites.

---

## 4. CROSS-FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT FRAMEWORK

Production, Quality, and Sales are currently locked in a zero-sum blame cycle because they optimize conflicting local metrics. Production is graded on labor efficiency (driving large batches); Quality on defect detection (driving caution/queue); Sales on bookings (driving aggressive promises). The following framework replaces siloed scorecards with value-stream ownership.

### 4.1 Unified Performance System: The “Triangle” Metrics
Every function is evaluated on a balanced scorecard. No single function can win unless all three metrics improve simultaneously.

| **Metric** | **Owner** | **Why It Matters** |
|---|---|---|
| **Quoted Lead Time Accuracy** | Sales | Sales must quote based on real APS capacity, not historical averages. Penalize for promising unachievable dates. |
| **Constraint Cycle Time (mech fab → final test)** | Production | Focuses Production on flow and bottleneck throughput, not labor utilization. |
| **First-Pass Yield + Warranty Cost/Unit** | Quality | Rewards Quality for *preventing* defects, not just *finding* them. |
| **Order-to-Delivery Lead Time** | **Shared (30% of variable comp)** | The North Star. Tied to cross-functional incentive pool. |

### 4.2 Governance & Operating Rhythm

**A. Integrated Business Planning (IBP) / S&OP**
- **Monthly Executive S&OP:** Sales presents the 3-month demand forecast; Production presents capacity and constraint status; Quality presents EQI trends and any emerging warranty risks. The output is a **unified Master Production Schedule (MPS)** that all three functions own.
- **Weekly Velocity War Room:** 30-minute stand-up with Production, Quality, Planning, and Sales ops. Visual management board shows:
  - WIP location and age
  - Orders at or approaching quality gates (with inspector capacity)
  - Material exceptions
  - Sales configuration freeze compliance

**B. Internal Service Level Agreements (SLAs)**
| **From** | **To** | **Commitment** |
|---|---|---|
| Sales | Production/Quality | Final configuration freeze within 48 hours of order entry; no post-freeze changes without Change Board approval. |
| Production | Quality | WIP arrives at inspection gates complete, with documentation, per APS schedule; no “dump and run.” |
| Quality | Production | Inspection TAT ≤ X hours (e.g., 24–48h) for standard products; inspector capacity planned in APS. |
| Production/Quality | Sales | Accurate available-to-promise (ATP) dates fed back to quoting engine within 4 hours. |

**C. Value Stream Manager (VSM) Role**
Appoint a **Value Stream Manager** (senior industrial engineer or operations leader) with dotted-line authority over Production, Quality, and Materials for a specific product family. The VSM owns the P&L proxy (cost, lead time, quality cost) and acts as the single thread through the functional silos.

**D. Joint Incentive Harmonization**
Move 20–30% of the annual bonus pool for Production, Quality, and Sales leadership into a **shared value-stream outcome**. If lead time drops to 8 weeks but warranty spikes, the pool is not paid out. If warranty is clean but lead time stagnates, likewise. Only simultaneous improvement unlocks full payout.

---

## 5. IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP

| **Phase** | **Duration** | **Focus** | **Key Deliverables** | **QLT Target** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 0: Baseline & Stabilize** | Weeks 1–8 | Current-state VSM; time-study validation; supplier lead-time audit; warranty FMEA update. | Validated time-loss model; certified inspection TAT baseline; supplier reduction roadmap; updated Control Plans. | Hold 14 weeks (stop the bleeding) |
| **Phase 1: Protect & De-Bottleneck** | Weeks 9–20 | Implement APS with quality-gate capacity modeling; launch supplier consignment/VMI pilots; establish weekly War Room; enforce configuration freeze SLAs. | APS live; 3 supplier VMI programs; internal SLAs signed; WIP supermarkets installed. | 11–12 weeks |
| **Phase 2: Flow & Parallelize** | Weeks 21–36 | Cellular layout pilots; inline inspection cells; OPP shift to ATO for top 20% SKUs; SMED events at constraints. | Flow cells operational; FPY improvement; ATO pilot proven; rework <2%. | 8–9 weeks |
| **Phase 3: Optimize & Extend** | Weeks 37–52 | Scale ATO/CTO across portfolio; advanced SPC; near-shore dual-source qualification; continuous improvement (Kaizen) cadence. | Full portfolio re-quoting logic; CCPM buffers tuned; win-rate tracking shows delivery-speed losses <10%. | 6–7 weeks |

---

## APPENDIX: KEY ASSUMPTIONS REQUIRING VALIDATION

1. **Demand Volatility:** The plan assumes 60%+ of volume can be standardized into CTO/ATO modules. If every order is uniquely engineered, the OPP shift will require deeper engineering transformation.
2. **Inspector Capacity:** The schedule protection model assumes 1.0–1.5 FTE certified inspectors per shift. If the company is understaffed by >30%, hiring/training is a Phase 0 prerequisite.
3. **Capital Availability:** SMED, cellular layouts, and MES/APS integration require modest CapEx. The business case (lost win rate × average deal size) should easily justify $300K–$800K investment.

---

**Next Step:** Commission the Phase 0 Value Stream Mapping and time-study blitz within 10 business days. The data will refine the week-by-week recovery targets, but the architecture above provides the evidence-based foundation for sustainable lead-time compression without repeating the warranty crisis.

--- ProcessRefiner ---
**OPERATIONS IMPROVEMENT PLAN: PROJECT VELOCITY & INTEGRITY (V&I)**
*Revised Edition — Lead-Time Compression with Certified Quality Fortification*

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The 14-week quoted lead time (QLT) is a construct of systemic delay, not manufacturing physics. Empirical benchmarks in discrete industrial equipment indicate that **value-added touch time is typically 1.5–2.5 weeks**; the remaining 11.5–12.5 weeks are consumed by queues, inspection bottlenecks, supplier float, engineering lag, and scheduling chaos. The competitor’s 6-week benchmark proves the art of the possible.

This plan provides a **feasible, risk-mitigated pathway** to compress QLT to **10 weeks within 4 months** and **7–8 weeks within 12 months**, while explicitly ring-fencing every certified quality gate and immunizing the business against a repeat of the prior warranty crisis. It is not a proposal to “go faster” by skipping steps; it is a system redesign to **remove the waiting time between value-added steps**, synchronize functions under unified governance, and replace batch-and-queue architecture with flow-and-postponement logic.

**Key Investment:** $400K–$900K (APS/MES integration, cellular layout, supplier programs).
**Key Risk Mitigation:** Pilot-before-scale on one Runner product family; a “Quality Surge” pause protocol if early indicators drift.

---

## 1. DIAGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT: THE 14-WEEK AUTOPSY

Before changes are made, a 30-day diagnostic blitz must validate the baseline. The table below moves beyond hypotheses to specify the **mechanisms of loss** and the root-cause logic required to target them.

| **Time-Loss Category** | **Estimated Weeks** | **Root-Cause Mechanism (The “Why”)** | **Diagnostic Validation Method** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Supplier & Material Float** | 4.0 – 5.5 | **MTO trigger delay:** Long-lead castings/forgings are not ordered until firm sales order (SO) entry, starting a 6–10 week supplier clock from zero. **Incoming inspection batching:** Material sits in receiving for 2–5 days until a batch threshold is reached for IQC. **Supplier opacity:** No visibility into supplier WIP; conservative internal padding added to every quote. | Time-stamp audit: PO release → dock receipt → IQC release for top 20 BOM items. |
| **2. Quality & Certification Queue** | 2.5 – 3.5 | **Unscheduled shared resource:** Certified inspectors are not in the formal production schedule; WIP arrives and waits. **Remote lab travel:** Physical transport from cell to central metrology/NDT lab adds 0.5–1.0 week. **Documentation friction:** Traveler packets are manually assembled, causing 1–2 day administrative delays before inspection can begin. **Fear-based reinspection:** Post-warranty-spike trauma causes inspectors to over-check or seek secondary opinions. | Track “Request for Inspection” to “Certified Release” timestamp (not just touch time). Map WIP buffer directly outside inspection areas. |
| **3. Inter-Operation Batching & Queue** | 2.0 – 3.0 | **EOQ-driven transfer lots:** Large lots are moved to “keep machines busy,” causing the critical path unit to wait for the rest of the batch. **Missing-component syndrome:** Kitting errors at assembly trigger emergent expedites that scramble priority. **Functional layout:** Parts travel long distances between departmental silos (machine shop → weld → paint → assembly). | WIP inventory turns by work center; track “travel distance per unit” and “queue time per routing step.” |
| **4. Engineering & Order Entry Latency** | 1.0 – 2.0 | **Post-order configuration:** Sales quotes custom variants that require post-SO ECOs, CAD/CAM reprogramming, and new BOM validation. **Tribal knowledge quoting:** No configuration guardrails in CRM/quoting tool; sales promises features that engineering must design after order acceptance. | Measure SO entry → engineering release (ECR) → production release cycle time. Audit % of orders with post-entry BOM changes. |
| **5. Scheduling Instability** | 0.5 – 1.5 | **Infinite-capacity MRP:** System backward-schedules from due date assuming unlimited machine and inspector capacity, guaranteeing overload and lateness. **Expedite addiction:** Sales and management override priorities weekly, creating Kingman’s Law instability (switching losses). | Schedule adherence %; count of manual priority overrides per week; measure “schedule jitter” (hours of planned work moved >48h). |
| **6. Rework / Hidden Factory** | 0.5 – 1.0 | **Prior speed-induced process skips:** The last lead-time compression effort reduced setup/validation time, injecting systemic defects (e.g., unverified weld procedures, missed torque sequences). **Late detection:** Defects found at final test force disassembly and loop-back. | First-pass yield (FPY) by work center; rework hours per unit; warranty root-cause Pareto linked to prior spike. |

**Critical Insight:** The longest path is not fabrication; it is the **serial accumulation of waiting time**. The 14-week quote is a defensive estimate that internalizes all of this waste. Recovery requires attacking the interfaces between operations, not merely asking individual departments to “work faster.”

---

## 2. PROCESS ARCHITECTURE: FROM BATCH-AND-QUEUE TO SYNCHRONIZED FLOW

### 2.1 Product-Family Segmentation & Cellular Flow
**Concrete Change:** Segment the portfolio into **Runners, Repeaters, and Strangers**. For the top 2–3 Runner families (typically 60–70% of unit volume), dismantle the functional departmental layout and install **U-shaped or L-shaped flow cells** (mechanical fab, electrical panel build, final assembly/test).

- **Pilot Constraint:** Begin with one Runner family to prove flow without disrupting the entire factory. The cell includes sequenced workstations with defined takt time.
- **Rhythm Wheel (EPEI) Scheduling:** At shared resources (e.g., large CNC, paint booth), implement a fixed-repeat cycle (e.g., every 3 days) rather than demand-driven batch accumulation. This stabilizes WIP and makes lead times deterministic.
- **Parallel Path Mapping:** Explicitly map non-dependent streams. Example: Control panel assembly and frame weldment proceed in parallel; they converge at a defined **integration event** with a time buffer. This can collapse 1.0–1.5 weeks of serial critical-path time.

### 2.2 Sales Configuration Guardrails & Engineer-to-Order (ETO) Discipline
**Concrete Change:** Hard-code an **80/20 Configure-to-Order (CTO) architecture** into the quoting engine.

- **Standard Module Library:** Engineering pre-validates mechanical, electrical, and software modules. Sales configures from this library; the system auto-generates a release-ready BOM and routing.
- **ETO Firewall:** Any request outside the module library triggers a mandatory Deal Desk review (Production + Quality + Engineering). ETO variants are quoted at 14+ weeks and priced with an engineering premium. This creates a **demand-shaping** mechanism that protects the value stream from post-order ECOs.
- **48-Hour Configuration Freeze SLA:** Sales must lock configuration within 48 hours of order entry. Post-freeze changes require a formal Change Board approval and automatic lead-time extension. No exceptions.

### 2.3 Setup Reduction (SMED) at Constraints
**Concrete Change:** Launch SMED events at the top 3 constraint operations (e.g., CNC tombstone changeover, paint color change, test-stand swap).

- **Target:** Reduce changeover time by ≥50% (e.g., from 90 minutes to 30 minutes).
- **Impact:** Lower economic order quantities (EOQ) enable single-piece or small-lot flow, directly attacking the inter-operation queue.

---

## 3. INVENTORY & POSTPONEMENT STRATEGY: STRATEGIC DECOUPLING

The objective is to absorb variance without building speculative finished goods. This is achieved by **shifting the Order Penetration Point (OPP)** downstream via strategically placed supermarkets.

### 3.1 Decoupling Matrix & Supermarket Sizing
| **Decoupling Point** | **Inventory Policy** | **Purpose** | **Sizing Logic** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Long-Lead Raw Materials** (castings, forgings, special drives) | Supplier consignment / VMI | Collapse supplier float; material available upon SO release. | **Max** = Demand during replenishment lead time + Safety Stock (SS); **Min** = SS; trigger = consumption signal. |
| **Pre-Kitted Sub-Assemblies** (pump modules, control bases) | WIP Supermarket (ATO buffer) | Decouple mechanical fabrication from final assembly; protect assembly from upstream variance. | 75th percentile weekly demand × (upstream lead time + 1 week SS). Replenished via kanban. |
| **Pre-Inspected WIP** | Quality buffer supermarket | Protect final assembly from inspection variance. | 3–5 days of downstream demand (small, because inspection is internal). |
| **Finished Goods** (top Runner SKUs only) | FG buffer | Instant fulfillment for highest-volume, speed-sensitive configurations. | 2–3 weeks of forward cover for Runner configurations only. |

### 3.2 Assemble-to-Order (ATO) Shift
**Concrete Change:** For Runner SKUs, pre-fabricate and pre-inspect all long-lead modules. Upon SO entry, final assembly and test begin immediately. This shifts the OPP from raw-material procurement to final configuration.

- **Working Capital Mitigation:** Offset FG/WIP carrying costs through supplier consignment (pay on consumption) and reduced expedite freight.
- **Risk Control:** Runner selection is based on 12-month demand volatility (CV < 0.5); Strangers remain MTO to avoid obsolescence.

---

## 4. SCHEDULING & CONTROL: FINITE SYNCHRONIZATION WITH PROTECTED QUALITY GATES

The prior warranty spike was caused by schedule pressure overriding process discipline. The new scheduling paradigm **embeds quality as a planned constraint**, not an afterthought.

### 4.1 Advanced Planning & Scheduling (APS) with Quality-Gate Capacity Modeling
**Concrete Change:** Replace infinite-capacity MRP with a finite APS that models:
- Machine centers (true available hours).
- **Certified inspection resources** (CMM time, NDT bay time, certified inspector hours).
- Tooling and fixture availability.

**Logic:** When an order is released, the APS forward-schedules through all operations, **reserving inspection slots** at certified gates. The quoted lead time is derived from the synchronized finite schedule, not backward-scheduling fantasy.

### 4.2 Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) Integration
Treat each order as a project:
- **Feeding Buffers:** Place time buffers (e.g., 2–3 days) immediately before quality gates and final assembly. This absorbs upstream variance without padding every operation.
- **Project Buffer:** A 3–5 day buffer before the customer ship date protects the committed promise date.
- **Buffer Management:** Daily War Room reviews buffer penetration (green/yellow/red). If a feeding buffer is >50% consumed, trigger a cross-functional response before the critical path is hit.

### 4.3 Frozen Zone & Expedite Governance
**Concrete Change:** Institute a 2-week **frozen schedule** (no changes to released work) and a 2-week **slushy schedule** (changes only via Deal Desk).

- **Expedite Protocol:** Only the COO can authorize an expedite. Authorization requires:
  1. Quality Risk Review (what gates, if any, are under pressure?).
  2. Impact statement (which 3 other orders are delayed?).
  3. Warranty Risk Board sign-off if any control plan modifications are requested.
- **No “Dump and Run” Rule:** Production cannot push WIP to a quality gate unless the traveler is 100% complete and the APS inspection slot is confirmed.

### 4.4 Available-to-Promise (ATP) / Capable-to-Promise (CTP) Quoting
**Concrete Change:** Integrate APS into the CRM quoting engine.
- **ATP:** If SKU is in FG or ATO supermarket, quote immediate availability.
- **CTP:** If MTO or custom, the APS runs a finite simulation and returns a date based on actual constraint capacity (including inspection load). Sales quotes the system date—never a “hope” date.

---

## 5. SUPPLIER INTEGRATION & PROCUREMENT TRANSFORMATION

### 5.1 Supplier Tiering & Incoming Inspection Reform
| **Tier** | **Criteria** | **Receiving Policy** |
|---|---|---|
| **Certified Strategic** | Cpk ≥ 1.33 on CTQs; annual audit; digital cert pack. | **Dock-to-line / Skip-lot.** Incoming inspection eliminated; material flows directly to cell or supermarket. |
| **Approved** | Standard PPAP; occasional minor non-conformances. | **Receipt-and-go** to supermarket with periodic sampling (e.g., 10% AQL). |
| **Development** | New or recovering supplier. | 100% inspection until promoted. |

**Concrete Change:** Reclassify top 10 suppliers by spend/lead time. Move qualified castings/forgings suppliers to Certified Strategic tier, removing the 2–5 day IQC queue entirely for those parts.

### 5.2 Capacity Reservation Agreements
Instead of spot-buying with 14-week lead times, negotiate **capacity reservation contracts**:
- Pay a 10–15% retainer to reserve forging/casting capacity by quarter.

## 6. QUALITY FORTIFICATION & WARRANTY RISK IMMUNIZATION

The plan institutionalizes the principle that **quality is the accelerator**. Certified gates are not bypassed; they are fortified, streamlined, and embedded into flow.

### 6.1 Zero-Bypass Gate Architecture
**Non-Negotiable Rule:** No certified inspection (CWI, NDT, CMM, hydrostatic, electrical safety) may be eliminated, abbreviated, or overridden by any authority. This is codified in the Quality Veto Protocol (see Section 7).

### 6.2 Certified Satellite Stations (Inline without Compromise)
To eliminate the remote-lab queue while preserving certification integrity:
- **Deploy satellite inspection bays adjacent to flow cells.** These bays maintain the same environmental controls (temperature, vibration, calibration) and traceability standards as the central lab.
- **Certified Inspector Rotation:** Inspectors are assigned to cell zones on a schedule published in APS. They perform inspections at the point of completion, not at a downstream tollgate.
- **Digital Pre-Positioning:** MES auto-populates the inspection packet (serial numbers, upstream SPC data, weld maps). The inspector begins metrology immediately upon lot arrival—zero administrative dead time.

### 6.3 Warranty Immunization Protocol
Based on the prior spike, implement these hardened controls:

| **Control** | **Specification** | **Prevention Mechanism** |
|---|---|---|
| **Spike FMEA Lock** | Update PFMEA/Control Plan to address exact failure modes from prior warranty event (e.g., specific weld types, torque sequences, software parameter sets). | Eliminates recurrence of known escape paths. |
| **Poka-Yoke at Source** | Install error-proofing at the defect origin: torque arms with digital capture, weld parameter interlocks, barcode-driven software loading. | Physical prevention of the errors that caused the spike. |
| **SPC with Automatic Stop** | Real-time SPC on CTQ variables (weld amperage, machining dims, torque values). Machine halts if Cpk drifts < 1.33. | Catches process drift before defect creation. |
| **First Article / Process Qualification** | First unit of any new/modified config undergoes 100% dimensional and functional validation. Serial production begins only after sign-off. | Prevents systemic defects from propagating. |
| **Layered Process Audits (LPAs)** | Daily audits by production supervisors; weekly by managers; monthly by directors. Checklist derived from spike FMEA. | Verifies that control plan is actually followed on the floor. |
| **Early Quality Indicator (EQI) Dashboard** | Track FPY, scrap, rework hours, test-stand retries, NCR rate by product family. Correlated quarterly to lagging warranty data. | Provides 4–8 week early warning before field failures manifest. |

### 6.4 Transition “Quality Surge”
During the first 90 days of any flow-cell or scheduling change, **temporarily increase inspection sample rates by 25%**. If FPY drops or EQI trends negative, trigger an immediate 2-week **Quality Surge Pause**:
- Halt further process changes.
- Root-correct the drift.
- Only resume flow expansion after validation.

**CRITICAL REVIEW: OPERATIONS IMPROVEMENT PLAN (PROJECT VELOCITY & INTEGRITY)**

**Overall Judgment:** The plan demonstrates strong theoretical command of lean enterprise, quality hardening, and supply-chain postponement. It is logically organized and recognizes the correct general categories of waste. However, from a manufacturing quality assurance and operational risk perspective, it suffers from a critical sequencing flaw—prescriptive architecture built upon unvalidated hypotheses—and contains latent risks that could inadvertently replicate the very warranty crisis it seeks to prevent. It requires revision before it should be authorized for execution.

---

### (A) CERTIFIED QUALITY INSPECTION GATES: EXPLICITLY PROTECTED, BUT PRACTICALLY DILUTED

**Strengths:** The plan uses admirably uncompromising language: “No Gate Elimination,” “Zero-Bypass Gate Architecture,” and a “Quality Veto Authority.” It correctly treats inspection as a planned capacity resource within APS, includes feeding buffers before gates, and mandates digital pre-positioning of documentation to eliminate administrative queue time rather than technical scrutiny time. The Warranty Immunization Protocol (Spike FMEA Lock, poka-yoke, SPC auto-stop) shows awareness that gates must be fortified, not merely preserved.

**Specific Weaknesses:**
*   **Inline/Satellite Certified Stations Risk Proximity Bias:** Moving CMM, NDT, or certified weld inspection from a central metrology lab into production flow cells—“satellite inspection bays adjacent to flow cells”—is a material change to the certified environment. The plan asserts that environmental controls and traceability standards will be maintained, but it does not address re-certification of these stations by the governing body (e.g., ISO 17025, customer source inspection, or third-party audit requirements). More importantly, it does not address *inspector independence*. An inspector physically embedded in a production cell, subject to daily social pressure from cell operators and a 4-hour TAT SLA, faces the exact proximity bias that erodes rigor. The plan’s “Quality Veto Protocol” is cultural; the embedded inspector’s reality is local.
*   **TAT SLAs Create Pressure to Rush:** Imposing a 24-hour (or 4-hour for Runners) inspection turnaround SLA on Quality, with a remedy that Quality must “add inspector capacity or accept scheduling priority override,” inadvertently recreates the schedule-over-discipline dynamic that caused the prior warranty spike. If Production knows Quality is on a clock, Production can weaponize the SLA to pressure marginal dispositions.
*   **Skip-Lot Confusion:** While incoming inspection skip-lot for certified suppliers is standard practice, the plan should more sharply distinguish between *receiving inspection* (conformance to PO) and *certified quality gates* (process validation, NDT, pressure testing). Blurring the two in implementation could lead to incoming material variance slipping into the value stream and degrading the very processes the certified gates are meant to validate.

---

### (B) ROOT CAUSES OF LEAD TIME LOSS: LOGICALLY PLAUSIBLE, BUT NOT EVIDENCE-BASED

**Strengths:** The six-category time-loss model (supplier float, inspection queue, batching, engineering lag, scheduling chaos, rework) is textbook-correct for industrial equipment. The plan acknowledges that value-added touch time is a small fraction of the 14-week quote. The emphasis on queue time, Kingman’s Law instability, and MTO trigger delay reflects solid operations research literacy.

**Specific Weaknesses:**
*   **Hypotheses Presented as Findings:** The plan repeatedly uses conditional language—“likely resembles,” “based on symptoms described,” “hypotheses must be validated”—yet immediately attaches specific week ranges (e.g., 4.0–5.5 weeks supplier float) and builds a multi-hundred-thousand-dollar capital and organizational plan upon them. This is the opposite of evidence-based reasoning. Evidence-based root-cause analysis requires *actual* time-stamp data, VSM walk-throughs, and baseline FPY/warranty correlations *before* architectural prescriptions are finalized. The plan prescribes cellular layouts, ATO shifts, and APS implementation before validating whether the bottleneck is truly batching (2–3 weeks) or, say, an engineering release process that is actually consuming 5 weeks.
*   **Competitor Benchmark Misused as Causality:** The competitor’s 6-week performance proves market feasibility, but it is not diagnostic evidence of where *this* factory loses time. The plan leans heavily on the competitor benchmark to justify its waste assumptions, which risks mirroring the competitor’s solution architecture even if the root cause profile is different (e.g., this firm may have a uniquely tortured NCR process while the competitor had a supplier problem).
*   **Missing Data Streams:** The diagnostic table lists “Diagnostic Evidence to Validate,” but the plan does not reference existing plant data such as historical schedule adherence, actual supplier OTIF performance, or current warranty Pareto data. A credible Phase 0 should have been completed *before* the improvement roadmap was published.

---

### (C) AVOIDING THE PRIOR WARRANTY SPIKE: STRONG CONTROLS, BUT A PERSISTENT OVERRIDE LOOPHOLE

**Strengths:** The plan correctly identifies that the prior crisis was caused by schedule compression overriding process discipline. Its response—FMEA Lock on the exact prior failure modes, SPC with automatic stop, poka-yoke, Layered Process Audits (LPAs), and a “Quality Surge Pause” protocol during transitions—is precisely the kind of immunization a QA reviewer wants to see. The First Article/Process Qualification requirement and the EQI Dashboard demonstrate forward-looking risk sensing.

**Specific Weaknesses:**
*   **The COO Expedite Override Preserves the Failure Path:** The plan states that “Only the COO can authorize an expedite,” contingent on an impact statement and a Quality Risk Review. This is naïve. In the prior warranty spike, the pressure almost certainly came from senior leadership reacting to sales demands. Giving the COO a formal override button—with no higher escalation or board-level visibility—reinstates the exact authority path that caused the original defect injection. A credible anti-spike protocol would eliminate expedite overrides of certified gates *entirely*, or require a written CEO/Board notification for any gate bypass, making the political cost of override higher than the sales cost of delay.
*   **Major Process Changes Lack Qualification Protocols:** The plan advocates shifting to flow cells, ATO, and parallel processing. These are fundamental process changes. Yet it does not mandate a PPAP-style or equivalent formal process validation (e.g., IQ/OQ/PQ) for the new manufacturing architecture before serial production. The plan demands First Article for *product* changes but not for *process* layout changes that alter operator motion, environmental exposure, and sequence of operations. New flow cells can introduce new failure modes (e.g., vibration affecting CMM-adjacent measurement, or cross-contamination in merged cells) that are not captured by the legacy FMEA.
*   **Inspector Embedding Risks New Escape Paths:** As noted in (A), embedding inspectors into cells to save transport time is itself a process change that could degrade detection capability. The prior spike was caused by speed; this plan introduces speed mechanisms dangerously close to the detection layer.

---

### (D) CROSS-FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT: COMPREHENSIVE ON PAPER, CREDIBLY FRAGILE IN A FEUDING CULTURE

**Strengths:** The plan recognizes the root cause of dysfunction—conflicting local metrics—and proposes a sophisticated remedy: shared KPIs (30% pooled variable comp), IBP/S&OP cadence, a Value Stream Manager (VSM), a Deal Desk for ETO control, and ATP/CTP integration into CRM. The Internal SLAs are specific, and the “Iron Triangle” metrics are well-balanced.

**Specific Weaknesses:**
*   **Dotted-Line Authority Will Fail Without Solid-Line Backup:** In a culture where Production, Quality, and Sales “each blame the others,” a VSM with dotted-line authority is structurally powerless. Functional managers control hiring, performance reviews, and daily priorities. The plan does not designate an executive sponsor (e.g., COO or a dedicated Chief Transformation Officer) with *solid-line* authority to break ties and enforce VSM decisions during the 12-month transformation. Without this, the VSM becomes a facilitator, not an owner.
*   **Punitive SLAs Deepen Silo Hostility:** The SLAs include penalties such as “Production loses next scheduling priority slot” or “Sales commission deferred until delivery.” In a feuding environment, these punitive remedies will be gamed and will generate resentment rather than collaboration. Effective cross-functional alignment in a broken culture requires *joint problem-solving* protocols and neutral arbitration, not transactional punishment. The plan lacks a non-punitive escalation path (e.g., a neutral Lean/ Six Sigma steering committee) to resolve SLA disputes.
*   **Sales Shadow Quoting Is Unaddressed:** The Deal Desk and configurator guardrails are sound for formal quotes, but the plan ignores the reality of verbal promises, handshake agreements, and “customer intimacy” behaviors by field sales. If a sales rep can verbally promise a custom variant before CRM entry, the Deal Desk is bypassed. The plan needs a field-sales audit mechanism and a strict policy that non-standard commitments made outside the configurator are unbonded by Production/Quality.
*   **Quality’s Catch-Up Override Clause:** The SLA states that if Quality misses TAT, it must “accept scheduling priority override to catch up.” This is a massive misalignment mechanism. It signals to Production that Quality can be forced into expedited inspection, undermining the very culture of rigor the plan seeks to build.

---

### SUPPLEMENTARY SYSTEMIC OBSERVATION

**Implementation Sequencing Risk:** The plan intertwines Phase 0 diagnostics with Phase 1 prescriptions. It proposes spending $400K–$900K on APS, cells, and supplier programs while admitting that the “time-loss model” is still hypothetical. A risk-averse QA/operations reviewer cannot approve capital deployment against unvalidated baselines. The plan should be restructured to a **diagnostic-gated** approach: Phase 0 must produce validated, timestamped evidence of where time is lost; only then should the architectural levers be selected and funded.

---

**FINAL DETERMINATION:** The plan contains many correct elements and reflects mature operations thinking. However, its evidence base is premature, its certified-gate protections contain practical dilution risks under production pressure, its expedite governance preserves the prior failure path, and its cross-functional alignment relies on fragile dotted-line authority in a hostile culture. **It must be revised.**

  - **Inspector Independence:** Inspectors report **solid-line to the Quality Director**, not to the Cell Lead or Value Stream Manager. They rotate between pods on a schedule set by Quality, preventing social entrapment with any single cell.
  - **No Production Pressure:** The 24-hour (Runner: 4-hour) inspection TAT clock starts only when the traveler is 100% complete and digitally pre-positioned. If Production arrives incomplete, the clock resets. There is no "catch-up override" forcing Quality to accelerate. If TAT is repeatedly missed, the remedy is **neutral arbitration** (Lean Steering Committee) to add inspector capacity or smooth upstream arrivals—not a production priority override.

### 6.2 Digital Pre-Positioning & Objective Criteria
- MES auto-populates inspection packets (serial numbers, upstream SPC data, weld maps).
- Hardened fixtures, pre-loaded CMM programs, and digital pass/fail thresholds replace subjective judgment, reducing inspector paralysis while maintaining rigor.

### 6.3 Warranty Immunization Protocol
| **Control** | **Specification** |
|---|---|
| **Spike FMEA Lock** | PFMEA/Control Plans updated to address exact prior failure modes. |
| **Poka-Yoke at Source** | Torque arms with digital capture, weld interlocks, barcode-driven software loading. |
| **SPC with Automatic Stop** | Machine halts if Cpk drifts < 1.33. |
| **First Article / Process Qualification** | First unit of any new/modified config or new cell layout undergoes 100% validation before serial release. |
| **Layered Process Audits (LPAs)** | Daily (supervisors), weekly (managers), monthly (directors). Checklist derived from Spike FMEA. |
| **Early Quality Indicator (EQI) Dashboard** | FPY, scrap, rework, test retries, NCR rate. Correlated quarterly to warranty lag data. |

### 6.4 Transition "Quality Surge"
During the first 90 days of any flow-cell or scheduling change, increase inspection sample rates by 25%. If FPY drops or EQI trends negative, trigger an immediate **2-week Quality Surge Pause**:
- Halt further process changes.
- Root-correct the drift.
- Resume only after Quality Director validation.

---

## 7. CROSS-FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT: THE IRON TRIANGLE WITH TEETH

### 7.1 Solid-Line Authority: Chief Transformation Officer (CTO)
In a feuding culture, dotted-line authority fails. A **CTO** (or designated COO transformation role) holds **solid-line authority** over the Value Stream Managers and the program during the 12-month transformation. Functional managers (Production, Quality, Sales) retain solid-line control of their people but must defer to the CTO on value-stream prioritization and resource allocation during the program. After 12 months, authority reverts to standard line structure.

### 7.2 Value Stream Manager (VSM)
- Owns P&L proxy (cost, lead time, quality cost) for the pilot family.
- Controls cell staffing, scheduling sequence, and can override functional managers on value-stream priorities, backed by the CTO.
- **Stop-the-Line:** VSM or any certified operator can halt flow for suspected quality drift. Restart requires documented Quality disposition.

### 7.3 Shared KPIs & Incentive Structure
**30% of annual variable compensation** for Production, Quality, and Sales leadership is tied to a shared pool, paying out only on simultaneous improvement.

| **KPI** | **Weight** | **Definition** |
|---|---|---|
| Order-to-Delivery Lead Time | 25% | Actual weeks from SO entry to customer receipt |
| First-Pass Yield (FPY) | 25% | % passing all gates without rework |
| Warranty Cost per Unit | 20% | 12-month rolling warranty spend / units shipped |
| Sales Forecast & Config Accuracy | 15% | % orders with zero post-freeze ECOs; MAPE |
| On-Time-In-Full (OTIF) | 15% | % delivered complete by original promise date |

**Clawback:** If warranty cost per unit spikes above baseline for two consecutive quarters, 50% of the shared pool is forfeited.

### 7.4 Governance Cadence
- **Daily Stand-Up (15 min):** Cell leads, Quality inspector lead, Materials, Sales ops. Visual board; problems assigned before exit.
- **Weekly War Room (60 min):** Production, Quality, Sales, Planning, VSM. Agenda: APS adherence, buffer penetration, EQI trends, expedite log.
- **Monthly IBP/S&OP:** COO, VP Sales, VP Ops, Quality Director. Unified 3-month plan; strategic buffer decisions; portfolio rationalization.

### 7.5 Neutral Arbitration & Joint Problem-Solving
To replace punitive SLA gaming with collaborative discipline:

**Lean Steering Committee (Neutral Arbiter):**
- Chaired by the CTO with rotating membership (one senior rep from each function, none from the disputed cell).
- Convenes within 24 hours of any SLA dispute or repeated miss.
- Empowered to allocate temporary resources (e.g., add an inspector, adjust a buffer, retrain a team) and to adjudicate penalties if bad faith is proven.

**SLAs Redesigned as Joint Commitments:**
| **From** | **To** | **SLA** | **Joint Remedy (Not Punitive)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | Production/Quality | 48h config freeze; no post-freeze changes | If violated, joint root cause in War Room; repeat violations escalate to CTO for commission structure review. |
| Production | Quality | WIP arrives complete with MES traveler | If incomplete, joint Andon response; Production supervisor and Quality inspector review together. |
| Quality | Production | Inspection TAT per standard (clock starts on complete docs) | If TAT missed, Lean Steering Committee assesses if capacity, arrival smoothness, or documentation is the root cause and prescribes fix. |
| Planning | Sales | ATP/CTP response within 4 hours | Missed quotes logged; joint review of planning workload. |

---

## 8. IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP & GOVERNANCE GATES

### 8.1 Funding & Authorization Gates
| **Gate** | **Timing** | **Criteria to Pass** | **Capital Released** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gate 0** | Week 0 | Board approves Phase 0 diagnostic budget and CTO appointment. | $50K–$100K (diagnostic team, VSM consulting, time-study tools) |
| **Gate 1** | Week 8 | Validated time-loss autopsy; confirmed bottleneck; updated Spike FMEA/Control Plan; supplier audit complete. | Phase 1 capital: APS/MES integration, pilot cell, configurator |
| **Gate 2** | Week 20 | Pilot cell passes IQ/OQ/PQ; FPY ≥ baseline; EQI stable; ATO supermarket proven for Runner family. | Phase 2 capital: scale to 2nd family, supplier VMI, near-shore sourcing |
| **Gate 3** | Week 36 | 2-family performance at 8–9 weeks; warranty data clean; cultural metrics (SLA adherence, War Room attendance) healthy. | Phase 3 capital: full portfolio optimization |

### 8.2 Phased Roadmap
| **Phase** | **Duration** | **Focus** | **Key Deliverables** | **QLT Target** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 0: Baseline & Validate** | Weeks 1–8 | Empirical VSM; timestamp audit; Spike FMEA lock; stop unauthorized expedites; establish CTO and War Room. | Validated time-loss autopsy; certified inspection TAT baseline; supplier tiering map; expedite moratorium enforced; Go/No-Go at Week 8. | Hold 14 weeks |
| **Phase 1: Protect & Pilot** | Weeks 9–20 | Launch one Runner flow cell **only if Gate 1 passed**; deploy Certified Inspection Pod with independence protocol; APS live with finite inspection scheduling; 2 supplier VMI pilots; configurator v1.0; Quality Surge active. | Pilot family at 11–12 weeks; FPY maintained/improved; OQ/PQ passed; War Room ritual institutionalized. | 11–12 weeks (pilot) |
| **Phase 2: Scale & Synchronize** | Weeks 21–36 | Scale to 2nd Runner family; ATO for top 20% SKUs; SMED at constraints; near-shore source qualification; EQI-to-warranty correlation confirmed. | Two cells operational; ATO proven; rework <2%; buffer management tuned. | 8–9 weeks |
| **Phase 3: Optimize & Entrench** | Weeks 37–52 | Full portfolio re-quoting; continuous Kaizen cadence; authority transition from CTO back to line; win-rate tracking. | QLT 7–8 weeks; delivery-speed losses <10%; warranty cost flat or down. | 7–8 weeks |

### 8.3 Risk Mitigation & Rollback Triggers
| **Risk** | **Mitigation** | **Rollback Trigger** |
|---|---|---|
| Flow cell introduces new failure modes | IQ/OQ/PQ validation; Quality Surge sampling | FPY drops >3% vs. baseline for 2 consecutive weeks → revert to prior layout for root cause |
| Inline inspection pods lose independence | Solid-line Quality reporting; rotation; physical separation | Any inspector complaint of Production pressure → immediate rotation and CTO investigation |
| ATO/WIP buffer causes obsolescence | Runner selection by demand volatility (CV < 0.5); monthly aging review | FG/WIP >90 days old exceeds 5% of buffer value → pause ATO expansion |
| Expedite pressure returns | CEO-notification rule; public IBP disclosure | >2 expedites/month affecting certified gates → emergency governance review |

---

## 9. APPENDIX: KEY ASSUMPTIONS & VALIDATION CHECKLIST

1. **Demand Mix:** Assumes 60%+ volume can be standardized into CTO modules. Phase 0 will validate actual Runner/Repeater/Stranger mix.
2. **Inspector Capacity:** Assumes current staff is within 30% of required capacity. Phase 0 will validate; if gap is larger, hiring becomes a Phase 0 prerequisite.
3. **Capital Efficiency:** Total program investment of $400K–$900K is justified by win-rate recovery (1 in 3 deals lost × average deal size). Phase 0 must validate the sales funnel data supporting this ROI.
4. **Certifying Body Coordination:** Re-certification of satellite inspection pods must be coordinated with ISO 17025 registrars or customer source inspection authorities. Quality Director owns this liaison.

---

**Immediate Next Step:** Board authorization of the CTO role and Phase 0 diagnostic budget within 10 business days. No architectural changes commence until the evidence is in hand.

step_logs.name: OpsPlanBuilder
step_logs.system_prompt: You are a senior operations strategist and industrial engineer. Draft a comprehensive operations improvement plan for an industrial equipment maker that quotes 14-week lead times while a competitor quotes 6 and sales loses one in three deals on delivery speed. The draft must include: (1) a diagnosis of where time is actually lost in the value stream; (2) high-level, actionable recommendations for process, inventory, scheduling, and supplier changes; (3) a strategy that protects certified quality inspections and avoids repeating the prior warranty spike; (4) a framework to align Production, Quality, and Sales around the plan. Make the draft detailed, evidence-based, and structured for further refinement.

step_logs.name: ProcessRefiner
step_logs.system_prompt: You are an expert in lean manufacturing, supply chain optimization, and cross-functional operations. Take the current operations improvement plan and refine it based on any feedback provided. Ensure the plan: (1) substantially reduces quoted lead times without compromising certified quality standards; (2) identifies actual time-loss points with root-cause analysis; (3) specifies concrete changes to processes, inventory policies, scheduling logic, and supplier management; (4) fortifies quality gates rather than bypassing them; (5) includes a robust alignment mechanism for Production, Quality, and Sales with shared KPIs and governance. Integrate all feedback to strengthen feasibility, detail, and risk mitigation. Output the complete improved plan.

step_logs.name: QualityCritic
step_logs.system_prompt: You are a critical reviewer specializing in manufacturing quality assurance and operational risk. Review the operations improvement plan. Assess whether: (A) certified quality inspection gates are explicitly protected and not diluted; (B) root causes of lead time loss are correctly identified with evidence-based reasoning; (C) the proposed changes avoid the mistakes that caused the prior warranty spike; (D) a credible cross-functional alignment mechanism exists for Production, Quality, and Sales. Provide your FULL assessment with detailed reasoning, strengths, and specific weaknesses. Then on the VERY LAST LINE output EXACTLY ONE of these keywords: pass, revise.
